```{r load-data}
clean        <- readRDS(here::here("data/clean/sl_st_clean.rds"))
gmm_results  <- readRDS(here::here("data/clean/gmm_results.rds"))
jags_results <- readRDS(here::here("data/clean/jags_results.rds"))

n_pitches  <- nrow(clean)
n_pitchers <- n_distinct(clean$pitcher)
n_sl       <- sum(clean$pitch_type == "SL")
n_st       <- sum(clean$pitch_type == "ST")
years      <- "2022–2024"
```

# Motivation

Major League Baseball's Statcast system classifies every pitch thrown into one
of several categories. Around 2022–2023, a new label appeared: the sweeper
(`ST`). Wide-breaking, horizontally-dominant, thrown with a flatter spin axis
than a traditional slider — the sweeper became the pitch of the moment,
credited for the dominance of pitchers like Corbin Burnes, Freddy Peralta, and
a generation of analytically-informed arms.

But the sweeper is not new. Pitchers threw pitches with this movement profile
for years. They were just called sliders (`SL`).

Statcast's introduction of `ST` as a distinct label raises an empirical
question: does the sweeper/slider distinction reflect a genuine difference in
pitch characteristics and outcomes, or is it a taxonomic relabeling of a
continuum that has always existed?  This matters because the label is now baked
into pitcher evaluation, scouting reports, pitch design conversations, and
published research.  If sweepers and sliders are not meaningfully distinct,
analyses that treat them as separate inputs are systematically misspecified.

This paper addresses that question empirically, using
`r format(n_pitches, big.mark = ",")` SL and ST pitches thrown by
`r n_pitchers` pitchers from `r years`.

# Historical Context: A Precedent

This is not the first time MLB's classification system has drawn a contested
boundary.  The sinker (SI) and two-seam fastball (FT) were treated as distinct
pitch types from the introduction of Statcast through approximately 2020, at
which point MLB quietly deprecated `FT` and absorbed two-seamers into the `SI`
category. The sabermetric community had long argued the two were geometrically
inseparable [@dvorocsik2019].  The reclassification validated that view.

The sweeper/slider situation is the current version of this problem, with one
key difference: the boundary is being drawn more finely rather than collapsed.
We are asking whether a split that did not exist in the data three years ago
is real.

# Research Question

**Does the SL/ST pitch label predict outcomes above and beyond the movement
features themselves?**

We decompose this into two sub-questions:

1. **Geometric:** Do data-driven clusters of pitch movement profiles align with
   the SL/ST label? If not, the label is empirically unsupported as a
   classification boundary.
2. **Predictive:** After conditioning on movement features (horizontal break,
   induced vertical break, velocity), does knowing whether a pitch is labeled
   SL vs. ST tell us anything additional about outcomes (whiff rate, wOBA
   against, chase rate)?

If the answer to both is no, the sweeper/slider distinction is a taxonomic
artifact rather than a meaningful baseball fact.  If yes, the new label is
justified and analysts should treat the types separately.

# Data

Data come from MLB Statcast via Baseball Savant, pulled using the `baseballr` R
package [@baumer2023].  We retain all pitches classified as either SL (slider)
or ST (sweeper) across regular-season games from `r years`
(SL: `r format(n_sl, big.mark = ",")`; ST: `r format(n_st, big.mark = ",")`).
The analysis begins in 2022 because the `ST` label did not exist before then.

**Variables retained:**

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `pitch_type` | SL or ST (the label under scrutiny) |
| `pfx_x` | Horizontal movement (inches, relative to gyroball) |
| `pfx_z` | Induced vertical break (inches) |
| `release_speed` | Velocity at release (mph) |
| `release_spin_rate` | Spin rate (rpm) |
| `release_spin_axis` | Spin axis (degrees) |
| `p_throws` | Pitcher handedness (L/R) |
| `pitcher` | Pitcher ID (for random effects) |
| `description`, `events`, `zone` | For outcome construction |

**Key preprocessing decision:** `pfx_x` is sign-flipped for right-handed
pitchers so that glove-side break is always positive regardless of
handedness — the relevant movement direction for sliders and sweepers.  All
three movement/speed features are standardized ($\mu = 0$, $\sigma = 1$) before
modelling.  Spin axis is standardized and retained as an optional fourth GMM
clustering feature (see Section \@ref(stage-1-gaussian-mixture-modelling)).

Three outcome variables were constructed:

- **Whiff** (binary): swing-and-miss or foul-tip on the pitch.
- **Chase** (binary): swing at an out-of-zone pitch (Statcast zones 11–14);
  NA for in-zone pitches.
- **wOBA against** (continuous): linear-weight wOBA for plate-appearance-ending
  pitches, using `r years` average weights from FanGraphs.

# Stage 1: Gaussian Mixture Modelling {#stage-1-gaussian-mixture-modelling}

## Method

We cluster all SL/ST pitches in the space of `pfx_x` (glove-side, sign-adjusted),
`pfx_z`, and `release_speed` — all standardized — using Gaussian Mixture Models
(GMM) via the `mclust` package [@scrucca2016].  GMM is preferable to $k$-means
because it is model-based (the number of components $G$ and covariance structure
are selected jointly by BIC) and provides soft cluster membership probabilities.

Cluster–label alignment is quantified by the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI;
@hubert1985).  ARI $= 1$ indicates perfect agreement; ARI $\approx 0$ is no
better than chance.  A forced-$G = 2$ solution is also reported to directly
test the two-cluster hypothesis implied by the SL/ST dichotomy.

```{r gmm-flag}
spin_note <- if (gmm_results$include_spin_axis) {
  "Spin axis (standardized) was included as a fourth clustering dimension."
} else {
  "Spin axis was excluded from the primary GMM (movement and speed only); inclusion is reported as a sensitivity check."
}
```

`r spin_note`

## Results

```{r gmm-summary}
g_opt    <- gmm_results$fit_bic$G
mod_name <- gmm_results$fit_bic$modelName
ari_g2   <- round(gmm_results$ari_g2, 3)
ari_bic  <- round(gmm_results$ari_bic, 3)
purity   <- round(gmm_results$purity, 3)
```

The BIC-optimal GMM selected $G = `r g_opt`$ components
(model: `r mod_name`), suggesting the data support
`r if(g_opt == 2) "exactly two" else sprintf("more than two (%d)", g_opt)`
natural clusters in movement–speed space.

When forced to $G = 2$, the ARI between cluster assignments and the Statcast
label is `r ari_g2` (Table \@ref(tab:gmm-tab)).  Cluster purity is `r purity`.
The BIC-optimal solution yields ARI = `r ari_bic`.

```{r gmm-tab}
tab_df <- as.data.frame.matrix(gmm_results$tab_g2)
kable(
  tab_df,
  caption = "Contingency table: GMM clusters (forced G=2) vs. Statcast label.",
  booktabs = TRUE
) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

```{r fig-f1, fig.cap="Movement profiles for SL (orange) and ST (green) pitches, 2022--2024. Glove-side break is sign-adjusted for handedness."}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/F1_movement_scatter.png")
```

```{r fig-f2, fig.cap="Forced two-component GMM clusters coloured by Statcast label. Heavy mixing within clusters would indicate the SL/ST boundary does not correspond to a natural movement discontinuity."}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/F2_gmm_vs_label.png")
```

```{r fig-f3, fig.cap="BIC as a function of the number of GMM components. The dashed red line marks the BIC-optimal solution."}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/F3_bic_curve.png")
```

# Stage 2: Bayesian Hierarchical Model

## Model

For each outcome $y_i$ (pitch $i$ thrown by pitcher $j[i]$) we fit:

$$y_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_i,\; \tau^{-1})$$

$$\mu_i = \alpha_{j[i]} + \beta_x \tilde{x}_i + \beta_z \tilde{z}_i + \beta_v \tilde{v}_i + \beta_{\text{label}} \cdot \mathbf{1}[\text{ST}]_i$$

$$\alpha_j \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_\alpha,\; \tau_\alpha^{-1})$$

where $\tilde{x}$, $\tilde{z}$, $\tilde{v}$ are standardized pfx\_x (glove-side
adjusted), pfx\_z, and release speed; and $\alpha_j$ is a pitcher random
intercept allowing for the fact that some pitchers throw both pitch types.  A
logit link replaces the identity link for the two binary outcomes (whiff, chase).

## Priors

Following @kery2012, we use weakly informative flat priors:

$$\beta_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\; 0.001^{-1}) \qquad \text{for all } k$$
$$\mu_\alpha \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\; 0.001^{-1})$$
$$\tau_\alpha \sim \text{Gamma}(0.001,\; 0.001)$$
$$\tau \sim \text{Gamma}(0.001,\; 0.001)$$

Precision values are in JAGS parameterization (SD $\approx 31.6$ for the normal
priors).  Prior sensitivity is an acknowledged open question.

## Inference

We run 3 chains in JAGS via `jagsUI` [@kellner2021], discarding 5,000 burn-in
iterations and thinning by 5.  Convergence is assessed via the Gelman–Rubin
diagnostic ($\hat{R} < 1.1$ for all parameters).

The estimand is $\beta_{\text{label}}$.  **A 95% credible interval that includes
zero** implies the SL/ST label adds no predictive value beyond movement.
**An interval that excludes zero** indicates the classification carries genuine
predictive information.

## Results

```{r extract-beta-label}
get_label_summary <- function(fit) {
  s    <- fit$summary["beta_label", c("mean", "sd", "2.5%", "97.5%")]
  rhat <- fit$Rhat$beta_label
  c(s, Rhat = rhat)
}

label_tab <- bind_rows(
  as.data.frame(t(get_label_summary(jags_results$fit_whiff))),
  as.data.frame(t(get_label_summary(jags_results$fit_chase))),
  as.data.frame(t(get_label_summary(jags_results$fit_woba)))
) |>
  mutate(
    Outcome = c("Whiff rate", "Chase rate", "wOBA against"),
    across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(., 3))
  ) |>
  select(Outcome, mean, sd, `2.5%`, `97.5%`, Rhat)
```

```{r beta-label-tab}
kable(
  label_tab,
  col.names = c("Outcome", "Mean", "SD", "2.5%", "97.5%", "$\\hat{R}$"),
  caption   = "Posterior summaries for $\\beta_{\\text{label}}$ (ST vs.\\ SL effect). All $\\hat{R} < 1.1$ indicates convergence.",
  booktabs  = TRUE,
  escape    = FALSE
) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

```{r fig-f4, fig.cap="Posterior densities of the SL/ST label effect across three outcome models. The dashed line marks zero. Intervals straddling zero indicate the label adds no predictive information beyond movement."}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/F4_beta_label_posterior.png")
```

```{r fig-f5, fig.cap="Caterpillar plot of pitcher random intercepts (whiff model), top and bottom 20 by posterior mean. Bars are 95\\% credible intervals."}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/F5_pitcher_intercepts.png")
```

# Discussion

The two-stage analysis tests whether the sweeper/slider distinction is real at
the level of pitch characteristics (Stage 1) and at the level of outcomes
conditional on characteristics (Stage 2).  The GMM results reveal whether
movement–speed space contains a natural two-cluster structure that mirrors the
SL/ST label ($\hat{R}_{\text{adj}} \approx 1$ would support the distinction;
$\hat{R}_{\text{adj}} \approx 0$ would not).  The posterior distributions of
$\beta_{\text{label}}$ then test whether knowing the label adds outcome
predictability beyond what movement already captures.

Several limitations warrant mention.  (1) The `ST` label was introduced
partway through 2022, so some pitches thrown early in that season that would now
be classified as sweepers may still carry the `SL` label, introducing
measurement error in precisely the first data-year.  Restricting to 2023–2024
is a useful sensitivity check.  (2) The chase-rate outcome conditions on
out-of-zone pitches, which is itself correlated with pitch type, potentially
inducing collider bias; this should be explored.  (3) The Kéry & Schaub flat
priors on precisions may be less well-calibrated on the logit scale than in
ecological count-data contexts; prior sensitivity analysis is warranted.
(4) Handedness matchup (same- vs. opposite-side) is not included as a covariate
here, though sweepers are particularly effective against same-handed batters —
including a matchup interaction is a natural extension.

# Conclusion

Whether the sweeper represents a genuinely new pitch type or a relabeling of
the extreme end of the slider movement spectrum is an empirical question with
real consequences for how pitchers and analysts interpret the Statcast
classification system.  This study provides a principled two-stage framework —
geometric separability via GMM, then outcome predictability via Bayesian
hierarchical regression — that can be used to adjudicate the question and, more
broadly, to evaluate the validity of any Statcast pitch classification.
